notes.meaning: God orders a tribute to be collected from the soldiers' share of the spoils. Out of every five hundred captives or animals, one belongs to the Lord. The soldiers risked their lives in the fighting, so God required a much smaller share from them than from those who stayed behind.

The tribute taken from the soldiers was given to Eleazar the high priest as an offering to the Lord. This was called a heave offering, meaning a gift lifted up and set apart for sacred use. It supported the priests and served as a thank offering for victory.

From the half given to the rest of the congregation, one out of every fifty people and animals was set aside for the Levites. The Levites were the tribe assigned to care for the tabernacle, God's sacred tent. This was a larger share than the soldiers gave, because the Levites were numerous and the people had faced no danger in battle.

Moses and Eleazar the priest carry out everything exactly as the Lord commanded. The whole division of the spoils was guided by God rather than human desire. Their faithful obedience showed that the victory belonged to the Lord alone.

The total count of livestock taken from Midian was huge, including 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, and 61,000 donkeys. This was what remained after the soldiers used some animals for food on their journey home. These numbers show that the Midianites were a wealthy nomad people with vast herds.

The plunder also included 32,000 young women who had never slept with a man. These were the only Midianite captives spared from death. Such a large number reveals how large and widespread the Midianite clans were.

The soldiers received half of the captured sheep, which totaled 337,500. Out of this large flock, the Lord's tribute of one in five hundred came to 675 sheep. This careful counting showed how faithfully Israel honored God with the first part of their gain.

The soldiers' share also included 36,000 cattle, 30,500 donkeys, and 16,000 young women. The tribute given to the Lord from these was 72 cattle, 61 donkeys, and 32 people. These thirty-two young women were assigned to assist with daily tasks at the sacred tent.

Moses gives the tribute from the soldiers directly to Eleazar the priest, just as the Lord commanded. He did not keep any of the dedicated portion for himself. Giving this gift honored the Lord as the true provider and defender of Israel.

The other half of the plunder was set apart for the Israelite congregation who had stayed behind. Their share began with 337,500 sheep, equal to what the soldiers received. Even though they did not fight, God ensured that the whole community shared in the blessing.

The rest of the congregation's portion consisted of 36,000 cattle, 30,500 donkeys, and 16,000 young women. Dividing these spoils among all the tribes helped provide for the entire nation. It reminded the people that they were one family under God's care.

Moses took one out of every fifty people and animals from the people's share and gave them to the Levites. The Levites did not receive an ordinary share of the land, so these gifts helped support their work at the tabernacle. Moses completed every part of this distribution in obedience to the Lord.

The army officers come to Moses after counting all the troops under their command. To their amazement, not a single Israelite soldier was killed or missing after the battle. This complete protection was a miracle showing God's direct hand in preserving their lives.

The commanders bring a freewill offering of gold jewelry they had captured, including armlets, rings, and necklaces. An atonement means making things right with God, and here it showed their humility for past mistakes and their thankfulness for being kept alive. They gladly offered their best back to God for saving them.

Moses and Eleazar receive all the finely crafted gold jewelry from the commanders. In total, the gift weighed 16,750 shekels, which was a huge and valuable offering. It reflected both the great wealth of Midian and the deep gratitude of Israel's leaders.

Each soldier had taken personal plunder, keeping goods like jewelry and clothing for himself. These personal goods were separate from the livestock and captives counted for the whole nation. The officers gave their gold offering freely out of what they had personally gained.

Moses and Eleazar place the donated gold inside the Tent of Meeting as a lasting memorial. It stood in the tabernacle as a visible reminder of God's miraculous protection and the people's gratitude. Remembering God's past mercies strengthens our faith to trust Him in every new trial.
